messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts:
I see we have a whole meetup in NY dedicated to the "Matt trick".
As much as I like Matt and think he's brilliant, this "trick"
had a name in the literature that we should be using. And as
Matt pointed out, it was only a Matt trick --- he knows several,
including other variants of the non-centered parameterizations.

I also don't like things called "trick" --- they imply that you
need to trick the software into doing something, which has
seriously negative connotations (for me, at least)

OK, this must be my morning for ranting.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts: For my QMSS class, I have taken to calling things like the Matt trick an "implicit prior", which is a prior you put explicitly on a primitive in order to imply the prior you want on a transformation thereof in order to get computational benefits. It should have a name though. It seems as fundamental to HMC as data augmentation (which is a poor name) has been to Gibbs sampling.

just call it a "transformed prior"?

Because sampling is based on geometry in all of
Metropolis, Gibbs, and HMC, it seems quite important
everywhere for MCMC. Of course, different transformation
horses for different sampling courses.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts: I prefer “implicit” or possibly “induced” but not “transformed” (i.e., my preference order is the reverse of Bob’s). The trouble with “transformed” is that it sounds too mathematical: you have a prior, then it gets transformed by a change of variables. That’s mathematically correct but it hides the fact that, in many ways, the transformation is part of the prior (this is related to that 2004 paper of mine).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts:
Not at all --- on matters of statistical terminology I'm happy
to defer to you. (Well, maybe I'll keep saying "bias" even if
you'd rather I just say non-zero expected error, and I sneak the
odd "MAP" in when you're not listening. I have pretty much
broken myself of the habit of referring to a sample as being made
up of multiple samples --- a sample is a sequence of draws, end of
story.)

And that's not just so you'll defer to me on computational naming,
which is much less of a quagmire and which has a lot more wiggle room
for naming without confusing people. But I'll stand by Stanbox being
confusing to anyone who knows what an Xbox is. Now we could grab
a raspberry pi, give it to Ben, and get a Stanbox Mini back, or we
could do the same by jailbreaking a first generation Apple TV;
even better would be a case mod for a raspberry pi to produce a
StanWallWart.

I think I've been in e-mail too long today.

- Bob

parts:
For what it's worth I like 'implicit', or 'implied' maybe. I think it gives the right intuition (as well as being an appropriate description mathematically).

And if these sorts of computationally motivated transformations are going to remain important (which they probably will) I like the idea of teaching them as just being part of the model. In some sense there's a gap between the theoretical model and the model as programmed, but in many ways they're inseparable in any practical context.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts:
The way I think of these, there are two models in play:

1. The posterior we actually care about.

2. The density over which HMC is actually performed.

If there are constrained parameters, Stan already provides
a built-in (implicit?) transform to some (2). For example,
positive-constrained parameters are log transformed (with
Jacobian) to unconstrained ones.

Then we sometimes add additional (explicit?) transforms to ease
computation. For example, applying the non-centered parameterization
to a hierarchical prior.

I take it the implicit or implied prior is the one we place
on (2) given that we want to be able to inverse transform
it back to (1). Isn't that just going to be the original prior
times the absolute Jacobian determinant of the inverse transform?

I'm really not arguing about the terminology here, I just want
to understand it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts:
This is basically the correct perspective. Remember, that the posterior
is a probability _measure_, which is a parameterization-invariant, abstract
mathematical object. The Stan Modeling Language defines a
probability _density_, which is a non-unique, parameterization-dependent
function from R^{n} -> R. What this means is that a given model can be
represented different ways in Stan, and different representations have
different computational performances.

There’s nothing implicit or explicit or whatnot going on. It’s just the fundamental
ambiguity of trying to define measures via densities.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "Matt trick" vs. "non-centered parameterization"
parts: My point from my 2004 paper (also the talk that Mike saw me give in London) is that, when the parameterization changes, the model can change too, because we tend to use certain natural classes of prior distributions. Thus, it’s not _just_ that we have a fixed distribution that we want to sample from, with reparameterizations being computational aids. In addition, once we reparameterize and add prior information, the model itself typically changes, often in useful ways. That is, the Pinocchio Principle.
